physical_harm: Deceased suffered head injury leading to hemorrhage and shock, resulting in death; another victim received four incised wounds and a fracture of the left parietal bone
number_of_offences: Multiple offences charged, some upheld; the accused were convicted under Sections 302 and 307 read with Section 34 and 149 of the IPC
motive: Strong motive to commit murder due to previous enmity between the complainant party and the accused persons
key_evidence_accepted: The evidence of PW-5 Bhagwan Singh, the injured witness, was accepted as reliable and consistent. His detailed account of the incident was corroborated by other witnesses, and the court emphasized that the exaggeration in their testimony did not alter the main prosecution story.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses, including PW-5 Bhagwan Singh, as trustworthy despite their potential interest in the case. The court emphasized that the evidence of interested witnesses is not always suspect and can be accepted if found reliable.

legal_representation.accused: P.C. Agarwala, Ambuj Agarwal, Chander Shekhar Ashri

investigation_status: Charge-sheet filed, case committed to the Sessions Court

appeal_history.trial_court: Convicted under Sections 148, 302 r/w Section 149 and Section 307 r/w section 149 IPC
appeal_history.high_court: Acquitted four accused of all the offences; convicted others under different sections
appeal_history.supreme_court: Appeal dismissed, no interference with the impugned judgment

prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the accused were involved in a brutal murder due to previous enmity and land disputes. The evidence of the injured witness PW-5 was found to be reliable and consistent, and the eye-witnesses corroborated the prosecution's case. The court emphasized that the evidence of interested witnesses is not always suspect and can be accepted if found reliable.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the prosecution witnesses exaggerated their accounts and involved acquitted accused, suggesting that the truth and falsehood were inextricably mixed. They claimed that the accused were falsely implicated due to previous enmity and that the evidence of the prosecution witnesses was unreliable.
legal_principle_applied: The court applied the principle that the maxim 'falsus in uno falsus in omnibus' does not have the status of a rule of law in India and is merely a rule of caution. The court emphasized that courts should separate the grain from the chaff and not discard the entire evidence merely because some parts are found to be deficient.
precedent_relied_upon: Balaka Singh v. State of Punjab (1975) 4 SCC 511; Rizan & Anr. v. State of Chhattisgarh (2003) 2 SCC 661
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed based on the conviction that the accused were involved in a brutal murder, and the evidence of the injured witness and corroborating eye-witnesses was found to be reliable and consistent with the prosecution's case.
other_sentence_order: Appellant-Sheesh Ram was sentenced to life imprisonment and a fine of Rs.1,000/-, in default, to further suffer six months rigorous imprisonment and to suffer rigorous imprisonment for five years and a fine of Rs.2,000/-, in default, to further suffer simple imprisonment for three months, respectively. Appellant-Rameshwar and Appellant-Radhey received similar sentences.
